title: Can I trust the Bible?
seoTitle: Can You Trust the Bible? Honest Answers to Hard Questions
description: Can you trust the Bible? A pastor who came to faith from atheism on how its books were gathered, what the old copies show, and the passages that are hard.
summary: How the Bible came to us, what the old copies show, and what trusting it does and doesn't ask of you.
askedAs: how was the Bible put together
who decided what books are in the Bible
was the Bible decided at Nicaea
is the Bible the word of God
answer: Maybe someone told you the Bible was changed so many times that nobody knows what it first said, or that a council of bishops picked the books to suit themselves. Or maybe you believe it, you noticed two passages that don't line up, and you were taught that one mistake would bring the whole thing down. You deserve a straight answer. Some of the difficulties are real, and some of the Bible's defenders have claimed more than the evidence gives them. But the honest picture is stronger than the rumors. The books were recognized slowly by scattered churches, not voted in at Nicaea, and the most important places where the old copies differ are marked in the notes of modern Bibles. Start with the first four verses of Luke, then read his Gospel with your questions written down.
happening:
For some of you the question came from outside: a class, a documentary, a friend who called the Bible a game of telephone played across two thousand years. For others it came from inside the book, when the Gospels didn't tell Easter morning the same way, or a passage about war or slavery wouldn't square with Jesus. Some learned to distrust it from the way it was used on them. And if you were raised to believe one error would bring down the whole faith, every hard verse feels like a test you're failing.

The skeptic's account runs like this: we don't have the originals, the copies drifted, powerful men picked the books long afterward, and the stories contradict each other. Some of that is true. No original manuscript of any biblical book survives, the copies we have were made generations later, copyists made mistakes and now and then changed a word on purpose, and the Gospels do differ in detail. I came to faith from atheism, and I'd rather you hear those true parts from a pastor than discover them later. What the account leaves out is scale and timing. The New Testament survives in a great many copies, made in many places, and comparing them is how scholars see where a copyist slipped. And the councils came late, but the books didn't; the churches had read most of them for generations before any council wrote down a list.

From the other side, many of us were told the Bible is God's word, so stop asking. There's something right in that: Christians have always confessed that God speaks in Scripture, and someone who holds God at arm's length until every question is settled may never begin. But that answer can't explain why the Bible itself invites checking (Acts 17:11), and it leaves a believer defenseless the day a hard verse turns up.

The classroom adds a third account: the Bible is a library of human writings, gathered over centuries. That's true as far as it goes, and the Bible is frank about its own making. But whether God spoke through those human words is a question no study of old documents can settle either way.

So notice which question you're asking. Some are about the text: *do we have what was written?* Some are about history: *did it happen?* Some are about the hard passages: *how could this be right?* And some are about authority: *does this book get a say in my life?* Each has its own kind of answer, and you can be settled on the first while still wrestling with the last.

scripture.intro: In these passages a historian explains his method, a prophet's scroll is burned and written again, a letter makes the claim Christians call inspiration, and Jesus says what the Scriptures are for. None of this proves the Bible by quoting the Bible. It shows what kind of book this is, and what kind of trust it asks for.

passages.text: Many have undertaken to compose an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us, just as they were handed down to us by the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word. Therefore, having carefully investigated everything from the beginning, it seemed good also to me to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.
passages.reading: The writer we know as Luke opens with a sentence about method, as serious writers of his day often did. Without claiming to have been there, he says others had already written accounts, that the material came from people who were eyewitnesses from the beginning, and that he investigated everything carefully before setting it in order for Theophilus, to whom he also addressed Acts (Acts 1:1). We don't know who Theophilus was. We know what Luke wanted for him: certainty resting on testimony from people who were there. Luke offers you the same terms, setting out what the witnesses handed down and leaving you to weigh it.

passages.text: And as soon as Jehudi had read three or four columns, Jehoiakim would cut them off with a scribe’s knife and throw them into the firepot, until the entire scroll had been consumed by the fire. Yet in hearing all these words, the king and his servants did not become frightened or tear their garments. ... Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to the scribe Baruch son of Neriah, and at Jeremiah’s dictation he wrote on it all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.
passages.reading: Here the Bible tells how part of itself was written, and it's candid about the process. Jeremiah dictated the words the Lord had given him over many years, and his scribe Baruch wrote them on a scroll and read it aloud at the temple. When the scroll was read to King Jehoiakim, he sat by a winter fire and cut it away a few columns at a time, unafraid, though his father Josiah had torn his clothes at the reading of the law (2 Kings 22:11). Then the words were written again, and the chapter adds, without embarrassment, that more were added. The Bible shows you the human hands, and a word that outlived the king who burned it.

passages.text: For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty. ... Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation. For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
passages.reading: The second letter of Peter presents itself as the apostle's last words (2 Peter 1:14), though its authorship was debated in the early church and still is. It answers, in two ways, the charge that the story of Jesus is a clever myth. First, testimony: the writer says he was on the holy mountain and heard the voice from heaven (2 Peter 1:18). Second, the prophets, whose words came as men spoke from God, carried along by the Holy Spirit. That is the heart of what Christians mean by inspiration. A letter in Paul's name, speaking of the Scriptures of Israel, puts it in a phrase: “All Scripture is God-breathed” (2 Timothy 3:16). The church came to say the same of the apostles' writings. Yet the writers remain themselves: men spoke, and were carried.

passages.text: You pore over the Scriptures because you presume that by them you possess eternal life. These are the very words that testify about Me, yet you refuse to come to Me to have life.
passages.reading: Jesus said this in Jerusalem to religious leaders who wanted him dead for healing on the Sabbath and calling God his own Father (John 5:16-18). They pored over the Scriptures, and what he faults is that they stopped at the page. The Scriptures are testimony, he says, and testimony points past itself to someone. It's possible to defend every line of the Bible and never come to the one it's about, and just as possible to pick it apart for years and never come either. That's a hard word for people like me, who handle the Bible for a living. The Bible doesn't ask to be trusted the way a manual is. It asks for the trust you'd give a witness, who speaks so that you'll come to know the one they speak about.

whyHard:
Some of the distrust was earned, and not by the Bible. Christians have sometimes defended it with more confidence than evidence, with impressive numbers no one checked and a tidy answer for every hard question. A reader who finds the oversell loses trust in the book along with the argument, and in us, pastors like me included. It's easier to hand someone a confident answer than to say *I don't know*, and the easy answer fails people at exactly the moment they need it to hold.

Underneath sits an assumption about what a true account has to look like. Many of us, believers and skeptics alike, carry a standard borrowed from the courtroom and the lab: a true report quotes exactly, keeps strict order, and counts precisely. Ancient writers worked differently, and the Gospel writers summarize and arrange by theme, as their first readers expected. Even the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy, the best-known modern defense of the Bible's accuracy, drawn up by evangelical scholars and pastors in 1978, says that round numbers, topical arrangement, free quotation, and differing selections of material in parallel accounts don't count against inerrancy. Many supposed contradictions are measured against a standard the Bible doesn't claim, and that even those defenders don't apply.

There's a second assumption, about power. We suspect whoever controls a text, often with good reason, so a story of bishops picking books to protect their position hardly seems to need evidence. The real history is slower. Letters were read aloud in house churches and passed on to the next town (Colossians 4:15-16), and lists came late, mostly recognizing what the churches already read, with honest arguments at the edges; early in the fourth century the historian Eusebius still counted the second letter of Peter among the disputed books. A conspiracy would have been quicker. Serious historians put the charge more sharply: the books were kept by the side that won the early arguments. There's truth in that, since the churches openly measured each book against the faith they had received. Whether that was a faction guarding its power or a family recognizing a voice it knew is yours to judge.

The church's use of this book earned some of the distrust too. American preachers quoted it to defend slavery, and it has been used to keep wives in danger and victims quiet. Others have trimmed it until it could only agree with them. Both are ways of staying in charge of a book that claims to be in charge of us, and many who did these things preached from pulpits like mine. When someone says they can't trust a book used like that, they're telling the truth about us. Yet many of those it was used against read it for themselves. Frederick Douglass, who escaped slavery, wrote in 1845 that he loved the Christianity of Christ and hated his country's slaveholding religion, and he made his case with Jesus' words against the hypocrites of Matthew 23.

That's the deepest difficulty, and it's in us before it's in the evidence. We want a certainty that asks nothing of us, either proof that removes every risk or a dismissal that removes every claim. The Bible offers neither. It presents itself as testimony, which is how we know much of what we know about the past, and it's trusted the way people are: by hearing it out, checking what can be checked, noticing whether it tells the truth when the truth is costly, as when it records Peter's denials and David's adultery, and staying long enough to know. The Bible has survived a great deal of scrutiny. The question is whether we'll stay in the room long enough to be questioned back.

thisWeek.intro: None of this asks you to decide anything by Sunday. These are small, honest things to do with the actual book, a few minutes a day. Start the first one tonight.

steps.title: Read Luke's opening, then keep going
steps.body: Read [Luke 1:1-4](/study/bible/luke/1) tonight and notice what Luke claims and what he doesn't. Then read on, a chapter a day; there are twenty-four. Read it the way you'd read any serious account of the past, neither hunting for errors nor skipping past them, and keep a notebook beside you for every question and objection, however small.

steps.title: Look at the footnotes
steps.body: Open [Mark 16 in the Study Bible](/study/bible/mark/16) and read the notes on verses 8 and 9, which explain that the oldest complete copies of Mark end at verse 8. Then read the notes on [John 8](/study/bible/john/8) about the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11), and look at your own Bible's preface, which usually names the Hebrew and Greek texts behind it. The evidence is set out for anyone to check.

steps.title: Lay four accounts side by side
steps.body: Read the words on the sign above the cross in all four Gospels: Matthew 27:37, Mark 15:26, Luke 23:38, and John 19:19-20. Write down what differs and what doesn't. Is it a contradiction, or the variation you'd expect when four writers report the same scene, one of them noting that the sign was written in three languages? Harder cases will come, and learning to ask the question carefully is the point.

steps.title: Read the best case on both sides
steps.body: Don't settle this against a straw man in either direction. [Can We Trust the Manuscripts?](/theology/doctrine/textual-criticism) and [How We Got the New Testament](/theology/doctrine/nt-canon) set out the evidence, give the skeptical case in its defenders' own terms, and end with the author's judgment. Then read a serious critic in his own words. Bart Ehrman, a New Testament scholar who left the evangelical faith of his youth, argued in *Misquoting Jesus* (2005) that scribes changed the text, sometimes on purpose, and asked why God would inspire words he didn't preserve. Notice which of his facts you can grant, and whether his conclusions follow.

steps.title: Take your list to someone who won't flinch
steps.body: Sort your notebook into four piles: the text, the history, the hard passages, and the book's claim on your life. Then take it to a pastor, a teacher, or a well-read friend who can say *I don't know* without getting defensive. You're not asking them to make the questions go away, only to look at the evidence with you. If the first person can't, ask someone else.

moreHelp.body:
Most questions about the Bible call for reading and honest conversation with a pastor or a well-read friend. Sometimes the question carries more. If fear that you've misread the Bible, or that God can't forgive you, fills hours of your day with checking, rereading, and confessing that bring no relief, see a doctor or a licensed counselor as well as your pastor, and do the same if a heaviness has spread into everything else. If someone has used the Bible to control you, frighten you, or excuse hurting you, that is spiritual abuse, and your safety comes first; the help lines at the end of this page can help you plan.

To find a counselor, ask your doctor for a referral, check your insurer's directory, or ask a pastor which counselors they trust. A good Christian counselor will take your questions seriously without pushing you out of your faith or hurrying you back into certainty. Christian or not, make sure they're licensed in your state.
signs: Fear that you've misread the Bible or that God won't forgive you fills hours of your day, and no reassurance lasts.
A heaviness has spread past your faith to sleep, food, work, and the people you love, for two weeks or more.
Someone uses the Bible to control you, frighten you, or excuse hurting you. If you're in danger, call 911.
You've had thoughts of not wanting to be alive. Call or text 988 now.
The argument over the Bible has split your marriage or family into sides, and every conversation turns into a fight.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need to explain it all. You can say, *I'm in a crisis of faith over whether I can trust the Bible, and it's affecting my sleep, my mood, and my family. My faith matters to me, and I want someone who will respect that.* Ask whether they're licensed in your state and have worked with faith questions or spiritual abuse. If you're calling your doctor, describe what has changed in your sleep, appetite, energy, and mood, and for how long.
moreHelp.cost: Cost shouldn't keep you from help. Ask any counselor whether they offer a sliding scale based on income. Community mental health centers and university training clinics usually charge less, and many employers offer a few free sessions through an employee assistance program. Many churches keep a benevolence fund for needs like this, so ask. A pastor's time is free, and so is [the Study Bible](/study/bible) here.

helping.body:
If someone you love asks whether the Bible can be trusted, or tells you they've decided it can't, they first need evidence that the question is safe with you. Panic teaches people to stop talking. Find out which question they're carrying: the text, the history, the hard passages, the book's claim on their life, or a wound from how it was used on them. Only some of those are answered by a book.

Then be scrupulously honest. If you don't know, say so and look it up together. Never hand them a claim you haven't checked; an oversold argument that collapses later costs more trust than the question ever did.

I'm raising five sons, and I want each of them to know that no question about the Bible is too dangerous to ask at our table. If you're a pastor, teach your people how we got the Bible and what the footnotes mean before they meet it in a classroom or a documentary.
say: That's a real question. People have asked it for a long time.
I don't know, but I'd like to find out with you.
Nothing you ask about this will scare me off.
dontSay: Who's been putting these ideas in your head?
You're just looking for an excuse to sin.
The Bible says it, and that settles it.
helping.next: Offer to read Luke together and look at the footnotes side by side. If the distrust comes from being hurt with the Bible, don't argue the texts; help them find a counselor, and if someone at home still uses it to control or frighten them, ask how it's safe to stay in touch and point them to the help lines at the end of this page. If they mention not wanting to be alive, ask plainly whether they're thinking of suicide, stay with them, and call or text 988 together. Then give it time. Trust in a book, like trust in a person, is rarely settled in one conversation.

prayer:
God, I want to know whether you have spoken, and whether this book is how. I've heard that it was changed, that men chose it for their own ends, that it contradicts itself. Some of that is true and some isn't, and I'm tired of not knowing which. I've seen your book used as a weapon, and I need to know whether that was you or us.

You let Luke do his research. You let Thomas ask to see your hands. You let a king burn your words, and you had them written again. So give me honesty, in me and in the people I ask.

Keep me from believing a rumor because it's easier, or defending a claim I haven't checked. If I've made this book smaller than it is, or used it to keep you at a distance, show me.

I don't need to understand all of it tonight. If the witnesses are telling the truth, let me hear it, even if it costs me, and bring me to the one they wrote about. Amen.

faq.q: Was the Bible decided at the Council of Nicaea?
faq.a: No. The Council of Nicaea met in 325 at the emperor Constantine's call to deal with the teaching of Arius, who held that the Son was a created being, along with the date of Easter and church order. Its surviving records say nothing about which books belong in the Bible. The New Testament books were recognized gradually, as churches read them in worship and asked whether they came from the apostles and their circle and agreed with the faith handed down. The earliest surviving list of exactly our twenty-seven books is in a letter of 367 by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and regional councils at Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 affirmed the same twenty-seven.

Many people, over many centuries, writing in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek. Some books name their writers, as the prophets' books and Paul's letters do. Others never say, including the four Gospels, whose names come from early church tradition, and Hebrews, whose writer is unknown to this day. Scholars still debate who wrote several books, and they do it in the open. The Bible's own claim, made of the prophets and extended by the church to the whole, is that behind its many writers stands one source: “men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21).

faq.q: Has the Bible been changed over the centuries?
faq.a: It was copied by hand for centuries, so copyists made mistakes, and now and then one changed a word on purpose. No original survives, as with nearly every ancient book, but the copies spread to many regions, and comparing them usually shows where a scribe slipped. Most differences are matters of spelling and word order. A small number change the meaning, and modern Bibles note the best known, such as the longer ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) and the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11). No central Christian teaching rests on a disputed passage. The Dead Sea Scrolls, found near Qumran beginning in 1947, include a scroll of Isaiah copied before Jesus' time, about a thousand years older than the oldest Hebrew copies known before, and it agrees closely with the text behind our Old Testaments. Modern Bibles are translated straight from the Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek.

It has real difficulties, and you should be wary of anyone who says it has none. Many ease once you ask what kind of writing you're reading: poetry speaks in images, proverbs describe how life usually goes rather than making promises, and ancient biographers arranged events by theme and summarized speeches. When a second-century Christian named Tatian wove the four Gospels into one smooth account, the church as a whole kept the four, differences and all. Some cases stay hard. Matthew says Judas hanged himself and the priests bought a field with his silver (Matthew 27:5-7); Acts says he bought a field and fell headlong there (Acts 1:18). The usual harmonization is that his body fell after the hanging and that a field bought with his money could be called his. Some readers find that convincing; others think the writers drew on different traditions. The Gospels differ in details at the edges, not on the cross, the burial, the empty tomb, or the claim that Jesus rose.

faq.q: Is there historical evidence for the Bible?
faq.a: Yes, though it helps to know what kind. Archaeology has confirmed many places, rulers, and customs the Bible describes; a stone found at Caesarea in 1961 bears the name of Pontius Pilate, the governor who sentenced Jesus. Among the earliest written evidence for the resurrection is a summary Paul says he received and passed on, naming witnesses, including a crowd of more than five hundred, most of whom he says were still alive (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). But no excavation can show that God spoke or that Jesus rose, and for some events, such as the exodus from Egypt, the evidence is thin and scholars disagree about what that means. Distrust anyone who says archaeology has proved the Bible, or disproved it. History can show that these writers knew their world; whether they were right about God is the question they put to you.

faq.q: What does inerrancy mean, and do I have to believe it?
faq.a: Christians across the traditions, Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant, confess that God has spoken in Scripture and that it carries his authority. How far its truthfulness reaches into every detail is debated among faithful Christians; the question divides churches, not the faith. Inerrancy holds that Scripture, in its original writings and rightly interpreted, is without error in all it affirms, history included, because God cannot lie. Its defenders point to Jesus' words that “the Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35), and its comfort is that you can trust every part. Infallibility holds that Scripture never fails or misleads in what it was given to teach, the way of salvation and the life of faith, while its incidental details use the ordinary language of their time. Its defenders point to its stated purpose, to make a person “wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15), and its comfort is that faith doesn't hang on settling every detail. The Chicago Statement of 1978, the best-known defense of inerrancy, calls confessing it vital and warns that rejecting it has grave consequences, while denying that it is necessary for salvation.

slots.note: James came to faith from atheism. If he chooses to, he could add in his own words what he believed about the Bible as an atheist, what he found when he examined it for himself, and what changed, beside the closing paragraph on testimony. The page stands without it. Two linked library pages already tell a version of this in the first person and need his confirmation before anything here leans on them: the Test the Case intro (/tools/test-the-case?case=gospels) says he believed the popular objections as an unbeliever without checking them, and the essay Why Would Anyone Trust the Bible? (/writing/why-trust-the-bible, dropped from this kit in review) narrates his unbelief at length.

Where James lands on inerrancy and infallibility, and why, in his own words. The answer to What does inerrancy mean gives each position its verse and its comfort, names it a question that divides churches but not the faith, and gives no landing. Pages in his voice already land: the closing judgment of /theology/doctrine/inerrancy (confesses Scripture's total truthfulness and trusts inerrancy's instinct more than its apparatus), the closing judgment of /theology/doctrine/scripture (the highest view of Scripture's truthfulness, held with the infallibility and confessional writers' cautions), and the essay Inerrancy, Infallibility, and the Word You Can Trust (ties the Bible's truthfulness to its saving purpose). Any landing added here should agree with those, or they should be reconciled first.

As a father of five sons, what James would want a parent to know when a child comes home doubting the Bible, in his own words and without describing his sons' private faith. It would sit beside the sentence about questions at his table.

reviewed.notes: Second pass (editor), against docs/grow/CARE-PAGE-SPEC.md, docs/VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md, and the third-batch review brief, read above all as the skeptic would. Truth: every historical claim kept is ordinary, well-established knowledge (Nicaea 325 and its business; Athanasius's Festal Letter of 367; Hippo 393 and Carthage 397; Eusebius's disputed books, Church History 3.25; Chicago Statement Articles XIII and XIX; the Great Isaiah Scroll; the Pilate stone, Caesarea, 1961; Tatian's Diatessaron; Douglass's 1845 appendix and Matthew 23; Ehrman's Misquoting Jesus, 2005). Web access was exhausted in both passes, so no source URL was opened; open each once before release. Changes: the manuscript superlative (more copies, closer to the writing than any ancient book) became a qualitative description, and the skeptic's account now concedes that the copies we have came generations later; the FAQ on changes names Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11 and says no central teaching rests on a disputed passage, with no statistics anywhere; the Judas texts (Matthew 27:5-7, Acts 1:18) now state the difficulty and give the usual harmonization as one reading among others; Ehrman's case is stated at its strongest (scribes changed the text, and why would God inspire words he didn't preserve), and the sharper scholarly form of the canon charge (the winners kept the books) is conceded in part and left for the reader to judge.
